en: Instruction on the Calculations of Kālacakra.
Oṃ, homage to the Buddha!

Śaka year 1091; Mleccha year [540]; Śuddha year 364; uncorrected month-count 4368; corrected month-count 4502. Dividing by fire (3), sky (0), and planets (9)—that is, 903—the remainder is 221 years. Dividing again by sixty, the remainder is 41 years. This was composed when nineteen years had passed within the first cycle of sixty years; this is one alternative calculation for the constant of the first year. The time of Mañjuśrī is six hundred years after the time of the Tathāgata. From that, the time of the Mlecchas is eight hundred years. From that time of the Mlecchas, subtracting one hundred and eighty-two years from the "sky-ocean-moon" (1040) years, one should calculate the constants for the months and so forth; this is the instruction. Furthermore, the nineteen years are not treated separately there for the purpose of inclusion.
Homage to the glorious Kālacakra!
Having paid homage to the one whose nature is Time, who is non-dual with that which is called Kālacakra,
this lamp is now illuminated for the sake of destroying the darkness of delusion.

In this context, the sixty-year cycle (*ṣaṣṭisaṃvatsara*), which consists of five hundred and twenty-three years, is to be calculated as follows: "The elapsed years, when multiplied by six and increased by sixty, constitute this ever-changing constant (*dhruvaka*). Thus it should be understood. To that constant of five hundred and twenty-three, the current year—beginning with *prabhava* and so forth—must be added as an additive (*kṣepa*). In this way, the sixty years beginning with *prabhava* are established.
Having added nine, eight, and four, one should illuminate [the result] by means of zero, five, three, and three.
"Having added [the result] to the Śaka kings' [era], and having subtracted from sixty, [one obtains] the years beginning with Prabhava.

This is its meaning: the elapsed years in the reign of the king known as Śaka are to be multiplied by eleven, and then multiplied again by four; having added nine, eight, and four, they are to be increased by four hundred and eighty-nine.

"One should cause to shine with the voids, arrows, and fires" means: having divided by three hundred and fifty, the remainder of the division is to be discarded; the Śaka years, increased by the quotient and reduced by the remainder of sixty, become the Prabhava and subsequent years. The quotient—the full cycle of the sixty years beginning with Prabhava—is not to be taken. The sequence of the sixty years beginning with Prabhava, starting from one (the Mleccha year) and so on, is well known by their respective names and is not written here for fear of increasing the bulk of the book. Thus, five hundred and twenty-three Mleccha years, including the Prabhava and subsequent years, are well known. These [years], when reduced by one hundred and eighty-two, are to be multiplied by twelve for the purpose of finding the months of the remainder. To find the current month, they are to be joined with the months beginning with Caitra. In this regard, the procedure is as follows: starting from the month of Vaiśākha, an addition of one and so on is to be made up to eleven. When the month of Caitra occurs, one year is to be added to the year-total and counted. This month-total is to be placed in two positions, one above the other, for the purpose of determining intercalary months (*adhikamāsa*). Here, due to the movement of the sun, when thirty-two and a half months are completed, one intercalary month arises. Therefore, thirty-two and a half months multiplied by four equal one hundred and thirty; or multiplied by two, they equal sixty-five. For the purpose of grasping the occasion of the intercalary month, whether the multiplier is four or two, it should be understood that the same applies to the occasioned impure or pure month-total that is to be divided. However, in the Tantra, it should be known that it is multiplied by four specifically for the sake of the meter. Therefore, the month-total is to be divided by one hundred and thirty or by sixty-five according to the previously stated method; the quotient obtained is to be added to the upper month-total as the intercalary month itself, and the upper [total] is to be made into a pure month-total. The remainder, because it is incomplete, is not to be taken. When nothing remains, then two [units] increase for the month. The increase of one for each month is added to the month-total; furthermore, it is certain that when there is an increase of two months, one intercalary month arises. Then, having added one month within that interval, the months are to be established in three places, and so forth—the three constants (*dhruvaka*) and so on—are to be calculated. Alternatively, in the three constants related to the elapsed months, one day (*vāra*) is to be added respectively to the days, thirty-two *ghaṭikās* to the *ghaṭīs*, two units to the total, one to the sub-total, and two constellations (*nakṣatra*) to the constellations, and eleven *ghaṭikās* to the *ghaṭīs*; thus the three constants related to the intercalary month are to be understood. The month-total increased by two months is to be understood as belonging to the upcoming month. This is the count of pure months.

Now the constant weekday (vāradhruvaka) is explained. The pure months should be placed in three positions, one above and one below the middle. Those in the upper position consist of weekdays; those in the lower position consist of *nāḍīs*; and those in the middle are for the purpose of determining the *ghaṭikās* of the weekday for each month. These [middle values] are multiplied by thirty-two. From the lower quantity, the quotient obtained by dividing by six is subtracted from the *nāḍīs*. The remainder of that division is multiplied by sixty; the quotient obtained by dividing by six consists of *pāṇīpala*s and should be written below the previously obtained value.

The remainder consists of six units; it is divided by six, and the quotient is in the form of breaths (*śvāsa*). That which is obtained from below should be subtracted from the upper portion, which is in the form of *nāḍīs*. One *nāḍī* situated below should be converted into sixty *pāṇīpala*s and then subtracted. One *pāṇīpala* situated below should be subtracted because it consists of six breaths. Thus, four positions are obtained through the sequence of higher and lower: the position of the day (*vāra*), which consists of a sixtieth part of a day; the position of the *ghaṭī*, which consists of a sixtieth part of a *ghaṭī*; the position of the *pāṇīpala*; and the position of the breath, which consists of a sixth part of a *pāṇīpala*. Therefore, six breaths constitute one full *pāṇīpala*, sixty full *pāṇīpala*s constitute one full *nāḍī*, and sixty full *nāḍīs* constitute one full day. This should be understood everywhere in this manner. This is the fixed constant (*dhruvaka*) for the calculation of sunset. For the purpose of calculating sunrise starting from the Sun and other planets, two days are added to the upper heap and thirty *ghaṭīs* are added to the lower heap. Having mixed the quotient obtained from dividing the heap of *ghaṭīs* by sixty into the upper heap, the day is determined by the remainder when the upper heap is divided by seven. When the remainder is one and so forth, the sunrise of the Sun and others is well known; however, the quotient, which signifies a complete cycle of days, is not to be taken.

Now, the constant value (dhruvaka) of the aggregate (piṇḍa) consisting of the days of the week is stated. The pure months, increased by one hundred and twelve, should be placed in two positions, one above and one below. From the lower [position], the quotient obtained by division by one hundred and twenty-six, when added to five, is to be applied as a positive quantity to the upper heap which has been doubled. For here, one month’s aggregate is produced by one hundred and twenty-six; there is an excess in the place of the aggregate due to the movement of the Moon. The remainder from the division of the upper position by twenty-eight constitutes the aggregate. However, the quotient, being of the nature of a revolution of the days of the week, is not to be taken. The remainder from the division by one hundred and twenty-six—the components of the aggregate—are to be placed below the aggregate.

Now the solar constant (*sūryadhruvaka*) is explained. The pure months are placed in three positions, one above and one below. Those at the top consist of *nakṣatras* (asterisms), those at the bottom consist of *ghaṭīs* (hours), and those in the middle are multiplied by eleven. From the figures in the bottom position, forty-nine is divided; the quotient, increased by two, is established as the nature of *ghaṭīs*. The remainder is multiplied by sixty and divided by that same [forty-nine]; the quotient, consisting of *pāṇīpala*s (minutes), is to be written below that. The remainder is multiplied by six and divided by that same [forty-nine]; the quotient, consisting of *śvāsa*s (breaths), is situated below that. For the quotients consisting of *pāṇīpala*s and *śvāsa*s, they too are to be increased by two as before. This is to be subtracted from the *ghaṭī*s in the middle heap, specifically from the place of the *ghaṭīs*; however, the aggregate of *pāṇīpala*s and *śvāsa*s is to be subtracted by descending further down—this is the uniform rule everywhere. Then, from the middle heap consisting of *ghaṭīs*, the quotient obtained by dividing by sixty is multiplied by two; this becomes an addition to the upper heap. Therefore, the remainder of the division by twenty-seven is the *nakṣatra*. The quotient, characterized as a revolution of the *nakṣatra*-wheel, is not to be taken. The figures situated below, consisting of *nāḍī*s (periods), remain as before. This is the constant of the pure months.

When one becomes weary of counting, then at each *vāra* (weekday), one should add one *vāra*; in the *ghaṭīs* of the *vāras*, thirty-two *ghaṭīs*; in the *piṇḍas*, two *piṇḍas*; and in the parts of the *piṇḍas*, two parts of a *piṇḍa*. In the *nakṣatras*, two *nakṣatras*; and in the *ghaṭīs* of the *nakṣatras*, eleven *ghaṭīs* should be added every month. This is the constant (*dhruvaka*) for the impure weekdays and so forth.

Now, the purification of the day of the week (*vāra*) and so forth is calculated, starting from the first day of the bright fortnight until the new moon, for thirty days. According to the sequence of the lunar stations (*candrapada*) and so on, these values—increasing by one—are to be added to the heap of days (*vārapinda*) and subtracted from the *ghaṭīs* of the weekday, taking the form of *ghaṭīs*. If the *ghaṭīs* of the weekday to be subtracted are not exhausted, then one should treat the weekday as sixty *ghaṭīs*, bring it down, and then subtract; this is the rule everywhere. Furthermore, when the weekday brought down, after adding or subtracting the lunar station and the solar [corrections], does not complete sixty *ghaṭīs* to become a full weekday, then it should be understood that the current lunar day (*tithi*) is being lost. In that case, having omitted that lunar day and assigned the next coming lunar day, all calculations should be performed. When, however, by virtue of the calculation the *ghaṭīs* of the weekday exceed sixty, then it should be understood that the lunar day is increasing. In that case, sixty *ghaṭīs* should be written under the current weekday, and the extra *ghaṭīs* should be written under the next weekday, until those extra *ghaṭīs* are exhausted. Once those extra *ghaṭīs* have been exhausted, the general rule applies as follows: when the heap is divided by fourteen, with an even quotient there is a credit (*dhana*), and with an odd quotient there is a debit (*ṛṇa*) to be understood. Among these, an odd debit is to be understood by a quotient of one or three, while an even credit is to be understood by a quotient of two or four. Even the absence of a quotient is considered even; one should understand that in the case of a debit there is a subtraction, and in the case of a credit there is an addition to the *ghaṭīs* of the weekday. Here, division by five and so forth does not occur, because when the heap is divided by twenty-eight, twenty-seven remains as the remainder, and no further excess exists. Therein, even if thirty lunar days are not yet given, there are not more than fifty-seven. And therein, division is possible only by four, acting as the divisor fourteen. The quotient obtained from the division by fourteen is not to be taken as representing credits or debits. Rather, the remainder of the division is to be understood as representing the lunar stations, ranging from one to thirteen. Having set aside the remainders from one up to thirteen which represent the lunar stations, the lunar station-pads should be understood in their respective order. In this regard, when one or thirteen remain after the division by fourteen, five lunar-day pads (*candravārapada*) are to be known. Likewise, when two or twelve remain, ten; when three or eleven, fifteen; when four or ten, nineteen; when five or nine, twenty-two; when six or eight, twenty-four; and when seven remain, twenty-five. And here, the solar [corrections] are to be added or subtracted just like the sun; if they were to be subtracted in the case of the sun, they are to be subtracted here as well.

Now, the previously mentioned lunar-day values (vāra-padas) have been combined. For the sake of easily understanding the operation of the multipliers (guṇaka), they are stated separately. Here too, if the remainder after dividing the total (piṇḍa) by fourteen is zero, nothing is to be added or subtracted; however, having multiplied the constituent part of the total by the first vāra-pada, which is five, and divided by one hundred and twenty-six, the quotient [is obtained].

One should practice [the calculation] together with the *vārapada* (weekday-position) of the Moon. As for the remainder, it is multiplied by sixty; the quotient obtained therefrom, consisting of *pāṇīpala* (minutes), is to be written below the *vārapada*. The remainder is multiplied by six; the quotient obtained therefrom is the total of breaths (*śvāsapiṇḍa*), which is to be placed even further below. In this manner, the arrangement (*nyāsa*) among those things to be described hereafter is to be understood. If one remains as a remainder, having omitted the indicator of the quarter (*caraṇapratipādika*), one multiplies by the *caraṇapada* situated below it; the previously stated rule applies. If two remain as remainders, having omitted two, they are to be known together with the preceding *vārapada*; when the constituent of the total (*piṇḍāvayava*) is multiplied by the five situated below it, the stated rule applies. When three or fourteen remain as remainders, together with the two preceding *vārapadas*, there are fifteen; when the constituent of the total is divided by the four situated below it, it is as before. When four remain, together with the three preceding ones, there are nineteen; when the constituent of the total is multiplied by the three situated below it, it is as before. When five remain, together with the four preceding ones, there are twenty-two; when the constituent of the total is multiplied by two, it is as before. When six remain, together with the five preceding ones, there are twenty-four; when the constituent of the total is multiplied by one, it is as before. When seven remain, together with the six preceding ones, there are twenty-five. Having made the constituent of the total into *pāṇīpala* and so forth by means of that which is situated below it, the quotient obtained by dividing by one hundred and twenty-six is to be subtracted from the twenty-five *vārapadas*. When eight remain, in all cases, having omitted the number indicating the quarter and having discarded the elapsed quarters, the twenty-four *vārapadas* situated in the six places—namely, the non-elapsed quarters—are to be written. In every case, in the case of retrograde motion (*utkrama*), having crossed over the middle line, one should discard the elapsed *vārapadas* and make the arrangement (*nyāsa*) by forming a collection of the non-elapsed ones; this is the proof (*pratyaya*). In the case of direct motion (*krama*), however, up to the middle line, the elapsed [and] the *vārapada* are combined and arranged; this is the distinction. Regarding the constituent of the total also, if it arrives in direct order, multiplication by the *vārapada* situated below the elapsed *vārapada* is desired; thereafter, the quotient obtained by dividing by one hundred and twenty-six is to be mixed with the *caraṇapada* according to the rule. But in the case of retrograde motion during the course, the quotient obtained by dividing the product of the constituent of the total—which is multiplied by the one situated above immediately after the elapsed one—by one hundred and twenty-six is desired to be subtracted from the *vārapada* according to the rule. When eleven remain, the non-elapsed [quarters] are situated in three places, amounting to fifteen. When twelve remain, the non-elapsed are situated in two places, amounting to ten. When thirteen remain, the non-elapsed is situated in one place, amounting to five. When the *vārapada* is zero, the stated rule regarding the division by fourteen applies. Even the fall of the *ravikā* (sun-shadow) is the same in this system regarding what is to be added or subtracted. All these *vārapadas* are to be understood as being added or subtracted according to the previously stated rule, having understood the even or odd movement, and the state of the *vāraghaṭikā* (weekday-minutes). These *vārapadas* have been written for the sake of showing beginners. Thus ends the purification of the weekday, lunar day, and asterism (*vāratithinakṣatraśuddhi*).

Now, the daily purification of the sun (*sūryaśuddhi*) is described. Starting from the first day (*pratipad*) of the bright fortnight, one should multiply thirty days by four, with each subsequent day increased by one. When that product is mixed with a third part, on the first *pratipad* there results four *ghaṭīs* plus twenty *pāṇīpala*s. That should be added to the fixed stellar value (*nakṣatradhruvaka*); this same procedure should be performed, increasing by one each day. Alternatively, four *nāḍīs* plus twenty-two *pāṇīpala*s should be added; this appears to be the pure [calculation]. Or else, according to the method of the Siddhānta, there are four *ghaṭikās* plus twenty-six *pāṇīpala*s and two breaths (*śvāsa*s); that is the fixed value consisting of the movement of the impure sun. Having established three values in the manner of "prior and posterior," one should understand that in one place there are six constellations plus forty-five *nāḍīs*, consisting of three signs. And thus, because the sun has been cleared by the three signs beginning with Aries (*meṣa*), Cancer (*karkaṭa*) emerges as the birth sign (*janmarāśi*). The remaining calculation for Mars should be understood in the same way as for the sun; however, the *cārapada*s (stations of movement) for Mars are different. For the sun, the *cārapada*s are four, four, and one: six in the first sign, Cancer; four in the second, Leo (*siṃha*); and one in the third, Virgo (*kanyā*). Then, in reverse order, one in the fourth, Libra (*tulā*); four in the fifth, Scorpio (*vṛścika*); and six in the sixth, Sagittarius (*dhanus*). The same should be understood for Capricorn (*makara*) and the others. Here, whichever *cārapada* arises, having raised the remainder of the multiplication by the next *cārapada* and made it a credit or a debt, one should divide by one hundred and thirty-five starting from the *ghaṭikā* position; the quotient, such as one and so forth, multiplied by six and so on, should be applied as a credit or a debt to the solar movement (*bhoga*). Due to the motion of the solstice (*ayanagati*), here in Capricorn and the following signs it is a credit, while in Cancer and the following it is a debt; this is the summary. It will be explained in detail in the *Upāṅga*. Thus is the daily purification of the sun. But there is no purity according to the method stated in the *Karaṇa*; and this is the method stated in the *Karaṇa*: in the first fortnight of Cancer, a debt of three *ghaṭikās*; in the second fortnight of Cancer, six. Likewise, eight in Leo, ten in Virgo, ten and eleven in Libra, eleven and ten in Scorpio, eight and six in Sagittarius, and three and zero at the end of the solstice. Thus, in Capricorn and the following, it is a credit; this is the intention in the *Karaṇa* and the Siddhānta. Thus, for six months, the hand (the sun) moves day by day through the divisions of the fortnights and transits (*saṃkrānti*).

Now, the purification of the moon is explained. Thirty lunar days (*tithi*), beginning with the first day (*pratipad*) and ending with the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), are to be added to the fixed asterism (*nakṣatradhruvaka*) in the place of the asterism for the purpose of increasing the asterism by one each day. Those same lunar days, converted into *ghaṭikās* and multiplied by six, are to be placed in another location; they constitute the *ghaṭikās* of the weekday (*vāra*).

The [nakṣatra] should be purified by means of these [subtractions]. Furthermore, those [values], having become thus, should be subtracted from the fixed nakṣatra (nakṣatradhruvaka) by means of ghaṭikās and so forth, according to their respective places; when this is done, those ghaṭikās and so forth belonging to the Moon’s motion become pure. The lunar nakṣatra-piṇḍa (the total number of nakṣatras traversed by the Moon) is the sum of the daily nakṣatra-piṇḍas—each increased by one—which are added to the fixed nakṣatra situated above. However, when the ghaṭikās and so forth to be subtracted from the fixed nakṣatra are not sufficient for subtraction, and the ghaṭikās and so forth to be subtracted remain as a debt (ṛṇa), then, by the force of calculation, sixty ghaṭikās should be added to the place of the ghaṭikās to be subtracted, and the aforementioned debt should be subtracted. Furthermore, one nakṣatra should be added to the fixed nakṣatra; it should be understood that the nakṣatra arrived at in sequence is thus lost. Consequently, in this case, having abandoned the nakṣatra arrived at in sequence, the upcoming nakṣatra should be written down. Then, the remaining ghaṭikās and so forth, purified of the debt, should be written down. When, however, by the force of calculation, the remaining ghaṭikās after subtraction exceed sixty, then it should be understood that the nakṣatra-ghaṭikās increase. In that case, sixty ghaṭikās should not be written down after the nakṣatra arrived at in sequence; rather, the excess ghaṭikās should be written down after the upcoming nakṣatra, as long as the excess does not diminish due to the force of calculation. When it does diminish, it follows the sequence exactly. When the ghaṭikās, being in excess, increase up to sixty, then it should be understood that one nakṣatra increases. Even then, sixty ghaṭikās should be written down in the upcoming nakṣatra until it diminishes through the loss of sequence. When they have diminished, it follows the sequence exactly.

Now, the twenty-seven yogas beginning with Viṣkambha are made clear. When the asterism situated above the fixed point (dhruvaka) of the lunar mansion and the lunar mansions traversed by the moon are added together, and when possible, twenty-seven is subtracted from the sum, the remainder constitutes the [current] yoga, such as Viṣkambha and the rest.

Now, the seven *karaṇas* beginning with *bava* are described. The lunar days (*tithis*) starting from the first day of the bright fortnight up to the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), numbering thirty, are doubled and increased by one; when divided by seven, the remainder determines the *karaṇa* starting with *bava*. Even if there is no remainder after division by seven, or if the remainder is one, it is still *bava* and the others in their respective order.

Thus, there are five limbs: the day of the week (*vāra*), the lunar date (*tithi*), the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), the conjunction (*yoga*), and the *karana*. The days of the week are the seven well-known ones beginning with Āditya (the Sun). The lunar dates are the fifteen each in the bright and dark fortnights, as they are well known. The lunar mansions are the twenty-seven beginning with Aśvinī, as they are well known. The conjunctions (*yoga*) are also twenty-seven, beginning with Viṣkambha. The *karaṇas* are seven, beginning with Bava. On the second half of the first day of the bright fortnight is Bava; on the first and second halves of the second day are Bālava and Kaulava; on the first and second halves of the third day are Taitila and Garaja; on the first and second halves of the fourth day are Vaṇija and Viṣṭi. Thus...

On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, *viṣṭi* occurs in the first half and *śakuni* in the second half. On the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), *catuṣpada* is in the first half and *nāga* in the second half. On the first day of the bright fortnight, *kiṃstughna* is in the first half and *punarvasu* in the second half. Thus, there are eleven *karaṇas*; this is the sequence of the fivefold limb (*pañcāṅga*). In the nine-quarter divisions of the asterisms beginning with Aśvinī, the twelve zodiac signs starting with Aries are well known. Their respective lords (*kṣetriṇaḥ*) are: Mars, Venus, Mercury, Moon, Sun, Jupiter, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Rāhu, and Jupiter.

Now, the constant values (*dhruvaka*) for the solar transits (*varṣasaṅkrānti*) are stated. The pure years (*śuddhavarṣa*), multiplied by eight and increased by four hundred, are diminished by the *karaṇa* years increased by eight. Divided by one hundred and seventeen (or divided by three hundred), they become the days of the week (*vāra*). The quotients, along with the remainders of the division, are multiplied by sixty for the sake of *ghaṭikās* and divided by the aforementioned [divisor]; the quotient becomes the *ghaṭikā*. Here, for the sake of determining the *karaṇa* starting from the Sun, two are to be added to the place of the day and thirty to the place of the *ghaṭikā*. The day of the week is obtained by the sixtieth part; the remainder of the division by seven is indeed the day of the week that occurs in the month of the solar transit of the year—this is the rule.

Now, regarding the addition [of corrections] during the transit (*saṅkrānti*) at Aries and the other signs, the additive values (*kṣepakāḥ*) for the fixed constants (*dhruvaka*) of twelve years are stated. For Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, and Virgo, there is one [unit] in the place of the weekday (*vāra*), and fifty-seven in the place of the *ghaṭikā*s. Here, the weekday in the place of the weekday becomes the additive when combined with the annual fixed constant; by that weekday, the transits of Aries, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces occur. As for the *ghaṭikā*s in the place of the *ghaṭikā*s, the rule is that they are applied as *ghaṭikā*s everywhere. There are four [units] in the weekday and thirteen *ghaṭikā*s for Taurus. One in the weekday and seventeen *ghaṭikā*s for Gemini. Four in the weekday and fifty-three *ghaṭikā*s for Cancer. One in the weekday and twenty-two *ghaṭikā*s for Leo. Four in the weekday and twenty-four *ghaṭikā*s for Virgo. Six in the weekday and fifty-one *ghaṭikā*s for Libra. One in the weekday and forty-seven *ghaṭikā*s for Scorpio. Three in the weekday and sixteen *ghaṭikā*s for Sagittarius. Four in the weekday and thirty-seven *ghaṭikā*s for Capricorn. Six in the weekday and forty *ghaṭikā*s for Aquarius. Zero in the weekday and fifty-two *ghaṭikā*s for Pisces. This conjunction of the transits is to be understood according to the cause. However, in the Siddhānta, this [specific] transit-enjoyment does not occur; rather, the rule is that one must determine the transit once the Sun has been purified in its jar (*ghaṭa*) by adding to the fixed lunar mansion (*nakṣatradhruvaka*) four *ghaṭikā*s plus twenty-two *pāṇīpala*s, increasing by one [unit] each day according to the previously mentioned method. By means of this fixed constant, a single year begins from Caitra; for the next year, however, another year is added, and by that, the interval between the fixed constants is established.

The Determination of the Transits (*saṃkrāntiniścaya*): Alternatively, from the beginning of the months of the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*), an examination must be performed for ten days by means of the shadow of a gnomon (*śaṅku*). From whichever day the gnomon’s shadow begins to turn northward, that is the day of the sun’s transit (*saṃkrānti*). [One should record] by that weekday, that lunar date (*tithi*), that conjunction (*yoga*), and that *karana*. On that day, the sun’s portion in the place of the asterism-portion (*nakṣatra-bhoga*) is twenty; in the place of the *ghatikas*, it is fifteen—this is the fundamental constant (*mūla-dhruvaka*). Into that constant, one should add daily the value obtained by dividing [the total] by the solar days of a cycle (*maṇḍala-dina*); thereafter, one should subtract the solar signs (*ravi-pada*) according to the previously stated method.

Now, the method for calculating the measure of the days of the mandala is stated: The number three hundred and sixty is placed in two positions; the lower one is doubled, and then the quotient obtained by dividing it by sixty-five is added to the upper position. The remainder is multiplied by sixty and divided by that same [sixty-five]; the quotient is to be written below the upper heap as *ghaṭikās*. Again, the remainder is multiplied by sixty and divided by that same [sixty-five]; the quotient is *pāṇīpalas* (seconds), which is written below that. The remainder is multiplied by six and divided by that same [sixty-five]; the quotient is *śvāsas* (breaths), which is written below that as well. Thus, having calculated the days and so forth, they are established in three places. From the *ara-daṇḍas*, there is an addition to the middle heaps by seven hundred and seven times seven (*707*) *ghaṭikās*. From the middle heaps, the quotient obtained by dividing by sixty-four is to be subtracted from the upper heaps. The remaining values are to be known as the days and so forth in their respective order. This is the purification of the solar mandala days.

Now, the daily motion of the Sun is stated: from the stellar wheel (nakṣatracakra), when multiplied by sixty, the quotient obtained by dividing by the number of days in its own mandala results in the ghaṭīs and so forth. In this way, for the others as well, the daily motion should be understood as the quotient obtained by dividing [the stellar wheel] by the number of days in their respective mandalas, according to the appropriate place. However, the daily motion of the Moon is derived from the nāḍīs of the other wheel; it consists of one hundred and thirty-three [nāḍīs], which, when mixed with its motion and divided by thirty days, results in the ghaṭī, pāṇīpala, and śvāsa units. As for the mandala-day of the breath-wheel (śvāsa-maṇḍala), the number of mandala-days should be understood by those daily motions—multiplied by however many [units] the stellar wheel is completed. The days, ghaṭīs, and pāṇīpalas for Mars’s mandala-days are six hundred and eighty-seven, plus one daṇḍa and forty-four pāṇīpalas. For Mercury, the mandala-days are eight thousand seven hundred and ninety-seven, plus one daṇḍa and [some] pāṇīpalas. For Jupiter, the mandala-days are four thousand three hundred and thirty-two. For Venus, the mandala-days are two thousand two hundred and forty-seven. For Saturn, the mandala-days are ten thousand seven hundred and sixty-six. For Rāhu, the mandala-days are six thousand six hundred and nine. As for Ketu, because it moves together with the Sun, its mandala-days are the same as those of the Sun. As for the daily motions of all [planets], they should be determined by dividing the stellar wheel by the number of days in their respective mandalas, according to the previously mentioned method. For Mars, [the daily motion is] in daṇḍas, pāṇīpalas, and śvāsas; for Mercury, in pāṇīpalas.
The *pāṇīpala* breaths of Jupiter are 3; of Venus, 3; of Saturn, 1 *pāṇīpala*; of Rāhu, 1 *daṇḍa* and half a breath; and for Ketu and the Sun, it is simply their own [mean] motion.

Now, the decrease and increase of days and directions during the southern and northern solstices are stated: this measure, consisting of three *pāṇīpala*s plus four breaths, should be understood to apply as far as Himavat on the northern side of Kailāśa.

Now the movement of Rāhu through the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) is explained. The months of the *karana* system, increased by one hundred and twenty-two, are multiplied by two for the sake of the heap of fortnights (*pakṣa*). For the purpose of the full moon’s movement, they are increased by one, having the nature of a single fortnight; for the new moon’s movement, they are increased by two, having the nature of two fortnights. For the sake of Rāhu’s fortnightly movement, these are divided by four hundred and sixty, which has the nature of a fortnight; the quotient obtained from the division is to be discarded. The remainder is multiplied by twenty-seven for the sake of the lunar mansions. From that, the quotient obtained by dividing by four hundred and sixty becomes the lunar mansion. As before, when multiplied by sixty and so forth and divided by this same number, the *ghaṭikā*s and so on are produced. By subtracting the days of the mansions and so forth from the cycle (*cakra*) in this manner, the remaining is the "mouth-Rāhu" (*mukharāhu*). The movements through the lunar mansions begin with Aśvinī. When combined with half the cycle, it becomes the "tail-Rāhu" (*puccharāhu*).

Now, the calculation of days for the purpose of determining the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) of the auspicious periods (*maṅgala*) and so forth is described. The months of the *karana* system, for the sake of calculating days, become days when multiplied by thirty. These, for the sake of the current [calculation], should be placed in three positions along with the preceding days starting from one, as before. To the lower heap, the quotient obtained by dividing by seven hundred and seven should be added as a credit to the middle heap. Furthermore, the quotient obtained by dividing the middle heap by sixty-four should be subtracted from the upper heap; this is the precise (corrected) number of days. The remainders from the division of both heaps are not to be taken. As for the lack of precision, it sometimes results in an excess of weekdays, which is not accounted for by those two [remainders]. For the sake of precision, an addition or subtraction of one should be made to one of them, and thus it becomes precise.

Now, the [calculation for] Mars is stated: The clear number of days, increased by one hundred and sixty-seven, is divided by six hundred and eighty-seven, which are the days of Mars’s mandala; the quotient, characterized as revolutions of the zodiacal circle (*nakṣatracakra*), is not to be taken. The remainder is multiplied by the zodiacal circle and again divided by the days of the mandala; the result is the asterisms (*ṛkṣa*). The nāḍīs and so forth are as before.

Now, the purification of Maṅgala is described. Here, when the occupation of the asterisms (*nakṣatra*) and so forth by Maṅgala is divided into its prior and posterior portions, there are nine and a half asterisms to be subtracted from a single occupation for the purpose of determining the birth sign (*janmarāśi*). This being the case, if the birth occurs in Leo (*siṃha*), [the calculation proceeds as follows]. If, in the occupation of the asterisms beginning with Aśvinī, the debt (*ṛṇa*) becomes excessive such that the quantity to be subtracted exceeds the available amount, then one should add a full circle (*cakra*) and then subtract. If the remainder after subtraction is greater than half a circle, or exactly equal to half a circle, then once half a circle has been discarded, the result should be understood as a credit (*dhana*) in the second Maṅgala-occupation sign, starting from the *ghaṭikā*s and so forth. When, after subtracting from the nine asterisms and so on, half a circle is not completed, then it is a debt. In this manner, it should be understood for all [planets]. If the remainder after subtraction does not even leave one asterism remaining, then one should multiply the *nāḍī*s and so forth by the first quarter-step (*caraṇapada*) and divide by one hundred and thirty-five—which consists of one sign and sixty *nāḍī*s. The quotient in *nāḍī*s and so forth, according to the stated rule, should be known as a credit or debt in the subsequent occupation sign. If the remainder after subtraction leaves an asterism remaining, then one should multiply that asterism by sixty, combine it with the heap of *nāḍī*s below, and then divide that heap of *nāḍī*s by one hundred and thirty-five. Having discarded the resulting figure (one and so forth) which indicates the quarter-step, one should mark the quarter-steps in ascending order starting from one. In that regard, having combined the heap of elapsed steps in the first half, one should multiply the remaining *nāḍī*s and so forth situated below that by five and so forth, and having performed the division, the quotient should be added; thus, it should be known whether a credit is to be given or a debt subtracted in the subsequent occupation sign. When, in the latter half, the multiplication is performed by the first quarter-step, then having combined the stated quarter-step, one should subtract from the heap of elapsed quarter-steps—after combining them—the quotient obtained from the remainder of the *nāḍī*s and so forth multiplied by the first step of the latter half. By means of the subtracted sum of elapsed quarter-steps, the credit and debt should be understood. Furthermore, when [the planet] passes beyond the zero-line (*mūlarekhā*) and the mark indicating the quarter-step, then one should discard the elapsed steps in the latter half and sum the unelapsed quarter-steps. One should multiply the remainder of the *nāḍī*s and so forth—obtained by dividing by five and so forth—by the first unelapsed quarter-step. Then, having again divided that product by five and so forth, one should subtract the quotient from the sum of the unelapsed quarter-steps in their proper place; the remainder itself should be known as the credit or debt. When the mark moves to the final quarter-step in the latter half, then having discarded that, one should multiply the remainder obtained by dividing by five and so forth by the first quarter-step of the former half.

Then, from that product, one should add or subtract the quotient obtained by dividing by five. This same principle should be understood as generally applicable to all subsequent cases that will be described. In the first half [of the verse], there are twenty-five steps for the quarters, eighteen in the second, and seven in the third; after drawing the middle line, one should understand the three groups of numbers in the latter half in reverse order. This applies everywhere. Then, in the fourth [half] there are seven, in the fifth eighteen, and in the sixth twenty-five. Thus ends the purification of Mars in the slow-motion calculation (*mandakarma*).

Now, the procedure for the fast motion (*śīghrakarma*) is explained. Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn—once purified by the slow motion (*mandakarma*)—are to be subtracted from the Sun when they are not already subtracted from it. However, in the case of Venus and Mercury, the Sun is to be subtracted from the positions of Venus and Mercury respectively. Here, the principle is that the slower planet is to be subtracted from the faster one. Mercury and Venus are faster than the Sun; the remaining planets are slower. For Mercury and Venus, the Sun is to be subtracted; for the others, the rule is as follows. In this fast motion, it should be understood everywhere that there is a credit (*dhana*) in direct order (*anuloma*) and a debit (*ṛṇa*) in reverse order (*pratiloma*). When half a cycle (*cakrārddha*) has been passed, it is a debit; when it has not been passed, it is a credit. Here, when half the cycle has not been passed, the remainder consists of numbers from one up to thirteen. Among these, starting from one, the numerical signs representing the units, tens, hundreds, and thousands—which remain—are to be deleted, and the figures should be written up to the position of thirteen. In the first half, the elapsed quarter-unit (*caraṇapada*) is multiplied by the first unelapsed quarter-unit in the second half; in the first half, the result obtained by dividing by sixty is added to the previous units and so forth to determine the credit or debit. In the second half, having subtracted the result obtained, one should add the total of the unelapsed quarter-units; here too, the credit or debit is to be known, and the rest is as before. The units of the days (*vārapada*) are: twenty-four in the first, then twenty-three in three ways, then twenty-one in two ways, then eighteen, fifteen, eleven, and three; then the root-line (*mūlarekhā*). Then: eleven, thirty-eight, eighty, and fifty-three.

Now, the purification of Mercury (*budha*) is described. The daily total (*dinapiṇḍa*), increased by one hundred, is multiplied by that same hundred and diminished by seven thousand two hundred and twenty-three. It is then divided by eight hundred and ninety-seven, the number of days in a [lunar] cycle; the remainder is as before. Then, the solar constant (*sūryadhrūvaka*) is placed in two positions—one before and one after—and in one of these, sixteen constellations and a half are to be subtracted. Thereafter, birth occurs in Scorpio (*vṛścika*). The rest is like that of Mars (*maṅgala*).

However, the *vāra*-padas are divided as follows: first, ten, seven, and three. Therein, from the root line (*mūlarekhā*), there are three; then seven, ten, sixteen, twice fifteen (thirty), fourteen, thirteen, eleven, seven, five, and zero. From the root line, there are four, eleven, twenty, twenty-eight, and thirty-four.

Now Jupiter is described. The root-sum of the days is divided by four thousand three hundred thirty-two, which is the divisor for the solar mandala consisting of one hundred twenty-six. The remainder is treated like that of Mars. When the motion of Jupiter has been calculated as before, twelve constellations are to be subtracted from one side; the remaining operations are to be performed like those for Mars. The sub-divisions of the weekday for the swift [motion] are nine, three, three, nine, and eleven from the root.

Now, the purification of Venus (*śukra*) is described. One multiplies the number of days by one hundred and divides [the product] by eighty-four, [and further] by two thousand two hundred forty-seven, which is the nature of the solar mandala. The remaining calculation is like that of Mars. For Mercury, when its solar constant (*sūryadhruvaka*) is set apart, six constellations (*nakṣatra*) are to be subtracted from one [revolution]. In the slow motion (*mandakārya*), the steps (*pada*) are five, four, one, and one as the root; in the fast motion (*śīghrakārya*), they are four and five. These are the steps for the weekdays (*vārapada*).

Now, the purification of Saturn (*śanaiścara*) is described. The total number of days is divided by four thousand eight hundred and sixty-six—the number of days in a *maṇḍala*—after subtracting one hundred and twenty from it. The procedure for the remainder is as in the case of Mars (*maṅgala*). Having separated the motion of Saturn as before, eighteen lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) are to be subtracted from one side; thus, birth occurs in Sagittarius (*dhanuṣi*). The slow-motion positions (*manda-cāra-pada*) are twenty-two, fifteen, six, six, fifteen, and twenty-two. In all cases, these are to be understood through retrogression (*viloma*). The fast-motion positions (*śīghra-cāra-pada*) are six, five, five, four, two, two, zero, and after the line of the root, two, four, five, six, eight, and three. Thus, the purification of the five planets beginning with Mars has been stated. Since the complete purification of the five planets beginning with Mars occurs through both the slow and fast operations, the purification is stated in both ways.

Now the characteristic of motion (*cāra*) is described. Here, the five planets have two types of motion: swift (*śīghra*) and slow (*manda*). Among these, when the five [planets] have risen from the solar disc and move in their regular order, it is called swift motion. The extent of the traversed degrees (*caraṇapada-bhoga*) continues until the base line (*mūlarekhā*). Slow motion, however, occurs during retrograde movement, and during westward movement when they traverse beyond the face (*mukha*, i.e., the base). Therefore, there is gain (*dhana*) by regular order, and loss (*ṛṇa*) when bypassing half the circle by reverse order.

Therefore, when moving in direct order (*anuloma*), it is called "swift motion" (*śīghracāra*); when moving in reverse order (*pratiloma*), it is called "retrograde motion" (*vakracāra*). When the Sun moves to the south, it is called "southern course" (*dakṣiṇacāra*); when to the north, it is called "northern course" (*uttaracāra*). When their light is eclipsed by the radiance of the Sun as they come near it, they are said to have "set. Mercury (*Budha*) and Jupiter (*Bṛhaspati*) are strong during swift motion; Mars (*Bhauma*) and Ketu are strong during retrograde motion; while Saturn (*Manda*) and Venus (*Śukra*) are strong only during retrograde motion. During swift motion, all [planets] face the east; during retrograde motion, they face the west.

Now the purification of Ketu is described: Ketu moves for thirty-six months at four and five *ghaṭikās* per day; that is, two *pāṇīpala*s and three breaths (*śvāsa*) each day. However, that which follows the sequence of the Sun to the east and is equal to the seventh [digit] from the Sun to the west, its rising occurs after three fire-months (*agni-māsa*). Its rising occurs within the mandala by distributing it through the distinction of eastern and western risings over those nine months multiplied by three. Then these [results] arise. [Thus ends the instruction on the calculation of Kālacakra.]
